h1: Sherry and raisin notes in aged beer and when they are welcome
title: Sherry and Raisin Notes in Aged Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: Why aged strong beers pick up sherry, raisin and dried fruit notes, the oxidation behind them and which styles welcome them.
teaser: In a ten year old barleywine, sherry and raisins are the reward. In a six month old lager, they are a warning.
standfirst: Sherry and raisin notes are what oxidation tastes like when it goes well. Strong, dark beers can age into something wonderful. Pale, delicate beers just taste stale. Here is the difference and how to tell which you have.
sections:
Sherry notes in beer sit somewhere between nutty, winey and dried fruit. Think of a dry oloroso sherry, a handful of raisins, prunes, figs or the dark fruit in a Christmas cake. In an aged beer they often come with toffee, caramel and a faint nuttiness like almonds or walnuts. The beer's colour may deepen and its hop bitterness soften.

These notes are oxidation flavours. Over months and years, small amounts of oxygen in the bottle react with malt compounds, alcohols and hop compounds, creating aldehydes and other molecules that taste nutty and winey. Our guide to oxidised beer covers the less pleasant end of the same process.

Strong, dark, malty beers have the raw material to age well. High alcohol slows spoilage. Rich malt gives plenty of compounds to transform into dried fruit and toffee. Dark malts carry natural antioxidants. Low hop aroma means there is little fresh hop character to lose. Instead of turning papery, they drift towards sherry, raisin and toffee.

Styles that commonly age well include:

  • Barleywine, both English and American
  • Old ale
  • Imperial stout
  • Belgian quadrupel and strong dark ale
  • Wee heavy and other strong Scotch ales

Most of these sit at 8% ABV or higher. A barleywine at 10 to 12% ABV can keep developing for many years in a cool cellar.
When the same notes are a fault

Sherry and raisin in a pale lager, a pale ale or an IPA mean the beer has aged beyond its best. Those styles are built on fresh malt and hop aroma and there is nothing in them that becomes better with oxidation. Instead of rich dried fruit, you get a thin, stale sweetness with papery or cardboard notes on top. Honey and toffee often appear first, as covered in our guide to honey and toffee notes in ageing pale beer.

So the same flavour can be praise or criticism, depending entirely on the beer. Judge it by asking whether the brewer meant the beer to be aged.

Oxidation, like most chemistry, runs faster in the warm. A widely used rule of thumb in brewing is that staling roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in storage temperature. A beer stored at 30 °C ages far faster than one at 10 to 12 °C and it ages less gracefully, because heat drives the harsher reactions too.

That matters in India. A barleywine left on a sunny shelf through a Chennai summer will not taste like one kept in a cool cupboard. If you want to age strong beer at home without a cellar, a wine fridge or the coolest, darkest corner of the house is far better than a kitchen cabinet.
What else changes as a strong beer ages

Sherry and raisin rarely arrive alone. Hop bitterness fades steadily, so a barleywine that tasted sharp and resinous when young can taste rounder and sweeter after a couple of years, even though very little sugar has changed. Fresh hop aroma disappears early. Carbonation can drop slightly. Colour deepens towards amber and mahogany.

With long ageing, other notes can follow: leather, tobacco, soy sauce or Madeira. In moderation they add depth. When soy sauce or wet cardboard takes over, the beer has gone past its peak. Our guide to leather and tobacco notes in long aged strong ales picks up that later stage. No beer improves forever and the best time to drink an aged bottle is usually a little sooner than collectors hope.
How to age beer for good sherry notes

If you want to try ageing beer yourself:

  1. Choose a strong, dark, malty style at 8% ABV or more.
  2. Buy at least three bottles of the same beer.
  3. Store them upright, in the dark, as cool and steady as you can manage, ideally 10 to 14 °C.
  4. Open one after six months, one after a year and one after two years.
  5. Write notes each time, paying attention to dried fruit, sherry, toffee and bitterness.

Storing upright keeps the yeast at the bottom and limits the beer's contact with the cap or cork. Darkness prevents light damage. Steady temperature matters as much as low temperature.

Beers aged in barrels that once held sherry, port or wine pick up winey, dried fruit notes from the wood as well. A barrel-aged imperial stout can taste of raisin and sherry partly from the cask and partly from slow oxidation through the staves. Our guide to tasting barrel-aged beer covers how to separate wood from age.

Your first step: buy three bottles of one strong barleywine or old ale, open one now and put the other two somewhere cool and dark with a date written on the label.
faqs: Why does old beer taste like sherry?
Slow oxidation over months and years creates nutty, winey and dried fruit compounds. Strong, dark beers turn these into pleasant sherry and raisin notes.
Strong, dark, malty styles such as barleywine, old ale, imperial stout and Belgian quadrupel, usually 8% ABV or higher.
Is a sherry note in a lager a fault?
Yes. In pale, hop-led or delicate styles it means the beer has aged beyond its best.
What temperature should I age beer at?
Cool, dark and steady, ideally around 10 to 14 °C. Warm storage speeds up staling and makes ageing less graceful.
